ai_summary:
Great Britain’s electricity network currently records total GB wind output of 6.3 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 2.8 GW, representing 27.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Despite zero-emission generation allowing Scotland to achieve an optimal Scottish carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh versus 208 gCO2/kWh GB-wide, severe north-south transmission bottlenecks prevent this surplus renewable power from reaching southern demand centres. 

Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 38.7 GWh via the Balancing Mechanism, incurring a constraint cost of about £1,338,738. Displacing this stranded clean volume required an estimated 7,357,237 m3 of gas burned elsewhere to replace it, needlessly releasing 13,553 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Annualising today’s balancing figures yields an estimated total yearly cost of £489 million for Scottish curtailment, which increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £1.80/MWh across national demand. These persistent grid boundary constraints leave consumers paying twice—initially to turn off inexpensive Scottish wind generation, and subsequently to fire up carbon-intensive thermal plant elsewhere on the system, undermining both cost-efficiency and national emissions targets.
